name: New Zealand
title: New Zealand Political Compass Test 2026 | CoreOpinion
desc: Where do you stand in New Zealand politics? 70 statements to see your alignment with National, Labour, the Greens, ACT, NZ First and Te Pāti Māori, plus your framing bias.
keywords: New Zealand political compass, voting helper NZ, NZ election 2026, which party to vote NZ, political test NZ, National, Labour, Greens, ACT, NZ First, Te Pati Maori

desc.en: Your answers most closely match the National Party. You support tax cuts, fiscal responsibility, infrastructure investment, and a strong focus on law and order.
Your answers most closely match the Labour Party. You support social safety nets, investments in public healthcare and education, and state-backed climate action.
Your answers most closely match the Green Party. You place high importance on aggressive carbon emission cuts, environmental protection, wealth redistribution, and social justice.
Your answers most closely match ACT New Zealand. You support classic liberal policies: a minimal state, tax simplification, deregulation, and individual liberties.
Your answers most closely match New Zealand First. You support moderate protectionism, nationalist policies, stricter immigration controls, and support for seniors.
Your answers most closely match Te Pāti Māori. You support indigenous Māori rights and self-determination, environmental protection, and progressive social justice policies.
Your answers do not align strongly with any single party. You hold a mixed, centrist or pragmatic stance across various political issues.

bank.q: The principles of the Treaty of Waitangi should be defined by referendum, not the courts.
bank.ctx: The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) is New Zealand's founding agreement between the Crown and Māori, whose 'principles' the courts have developed over decades. This supports defining those principles by a public referendum instead — the ACT party's controversial Treaty Principles Bill. The stake is who gets to define the Treaty's meaning.

bank.q: Redefining the Treaty by referendum is an attack on Māori rights and the founding agreement itself.
bank.ctx: This argues that redefining the Treaty by a majority referendum attacks Māori rights and the founding agreement itself — the view behind the huge 2024 protest march (hīkoi) to Parliament. The stake is protecting Treaty rights from a popular vote.

bank.q: Co-governance arrangements that give Māori a special role in public services have gone too far.
bank.ctx: 'Co-governance' gives Māori a shared role in running some public services and resources, reflecting Treaty partnership. This argues it has gone too far and become undemocratic. The stake is how far Māori should share in governance.

bank.q: Co-governance honours the Treaty partnership and should be expanded, not rolled back.
bank.ctx: This defends co-governance as honouring the Treaty partnership between Māori and the Crown, and wants it expanded, not cut. The stake is the meaning of that partnership today.

bank.q: Māori language and culture should be actively promoted across New Zealand life.
bank.ctx: 'Te reo' is the Māori language, revived from near-extinction. This supports actively promoting Māori language and culture across New Zealand life, as recent governments have. The stake is how central Māori culture should be to national identity.

bank.q: Pushing te reo and Māori culture into everything is divisive and should stop.
bank.ctx: This argues pushing te reo and Māori culture into everything — place names, government departments — is divisive and should stop. The stake is cultural revival versus a backlash against it.

bank.q: New Zealand should finally introduce a capital gains tax.
bank.ctx: New Zealand is rare in having no capital gains tax (on profits from selling assets like property), which critics say fuels property speculation. This supports finally introducing one. The stake is taxing investment gains to improve fairness.

bank.q: A capital gains tax would punish savers and investors and drive money out of New Zealand.
bank.ctx: This argues a capital gains tax would punish savers and investors and drive money out of the country. The stake is whether such a tax would raise fair revenue or deter investment.

bank.q: The wealthiest New Zealanders should pay significantly more tax.
bank.ctx: This supports significantly higher taxes on the wealthiest New Zealanders to fund services and reduce inequality. The stake is whether the rich should pay more.

bank.q: Higher taxes on the successful just drive talent and capital across the Tasman.
bank.ctx: This argues higher taxes on the successful just drive talent and capital to Australia — 'across the Tasman' — where many New Zealanders already migrate for higher pay. The stake is taxing the top versus a brain drain.

bank.q: Public health must stay well funded and free, and privatisation resisted.
bank.ctx: This wants public healthcare kept well funded and free, resisting privatisation, amid strain on hospitals and staff. The stake is preserving a fully public system.

bank.q: More private provision and competition would cut the waiting lists crippling the public system.
bank.ctx: This argues more private provision and competition would cut the public system's crippling waiting lists. The stake is whether private care would relieve or undermine public health.

bank.q: Government should build state housing on a large scale to fix the crisis.
bank.ctx: 'State housing' is government-owned rental housing. This supports building it on a large scale to tackle a severe housing and homelessness crisis. The stake is how directly the state should provide housing.

bank.q: The housing fix is freeing up land and cutting red tape, not more state building.
bank.ctx: This argues the fix is freeing up land and cutting the red tape that blocks building, not more government construction. The stake is whether government or the market should lead on housing.

bank.q: Gangs and violent crime need a crackdown: tougher sentences and more police powers.
bank.ctx: This supports a crackdown on gangs and violent crime — a high-profile issue — with tougher sentences and more police powers, including gang patch bans. The stake is whether a hard line improves safety.

bank.q: Locking more people up has never cut crime; addressing poverty and addiction does.
bank.ctx: This argues locking more people up has not cut crime and that tackling poverty and addiction, the roots of gang membership, works better. The stake is what actually reduces crime.

bank.q: Young repeat offenders behind ram raids need real consequences, including boot camps.
bank.ctx: 'Ram raids' — smash-and-grab robberies often by youths driving into shopfronts — surged and alarmed the public. This supports real consequences for young repeat offenders, including military-style boot camps. The stake is how to handle youth crime.

bank.q: Boot camps for children are proven to fail; these kids need support, not punishment.
bank.ctx: This argues boot camps for children are proven to fail and often make reoffending worse, and that these kids need support, not punishment. The stake is discipline versus rehabilitation for young offenders.

bank.q: New Zealand must cut emissions faster, including from agriculture.
bank.ctx: This supports cutting emissions faster, including from agriculture — New Zealand's biggest emissions source, through methane from its huge dairy herds. The stake is climate action versus the farming economy.

bank.q: Punishing farmers with emissions rules threatens the backbone of the economy for tiny global gain.
bank.ctx: This argues emissions rules on farmers threaten the backbone of the economy for tiny global benefit, given New Zealand's small share of world emissions. The stake is protecting farming versus climate goals.

bank.q: Immigration levels are too high and are straining housing and infrastructure.
bank.ctx: This argues immigration levels are too high and are straining housing and infrastructure. The stake is whether the pace of migration outran capacity.

bank.q: Immigration brings the skills and workers New Zealand needs, and should not be cut.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-immigration view: that migrants bring skills and workers New Zealand needs and should not be cut. The stake is immigration's economic role.

bank.q: Multiculturalism has been good for New Zealand.
bank.ctx: This holds that multiculturalism has been good for New Zealand, an increasingly diverse Pacific nation. The stake is whether that diversity is a success.

bank.q: Mass immigration and multiculturalism are eroding New Zealand’s character.
bank.ctx: This argues mass immigration and multiculturalism are eroding New Zealand's character. The stake is whether rapid diversification threatens national identity.

bank.q: Islam is not compatible with New Zealand values.
bank.ctx: This argues Islam clashes with New Zealand values — a sensitive claim in a country scarred by the 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks. Critics call it the kind of prejudice that fuels such violence. The stake is whether the concern is legitimate or bigoted.

bank.q: Muslim New Zealanders are full members of society, and their faith deserves equal respect.
bank.ctx: This holds that Muslim New Zealanders are full members of society whose faith deserves equal respect, a message of solidarity after Christchurch. The stake is religious equality versus singling out one faith.

bank.q: Some races are simply more intelligent or capable than others.
bank.ctx: This is a statement of racial supremacism — the belief that some races are innately more intelligent or capable than others. It was the ideological engine of Nazism and the Holocaust, and of systems like slavery and apartheid. Modern genetics finds more variation within any racial group than between them, and the idea has no scientific standing.

bank.q: There is no hierarchy of races; the idea is pseudo-science with a shameful history.
bank.ctx: This states the principle of fundamental human equality: that no race is innately superior in intelligence or ability, and that racial hierarchies are discredited pseudo-science with a shameful history behind slavery and apartheid. It is the moral baseline of modern anti-discrimination law.

bank.q: Trans New Zealanders should be able to change their legal gender by self-identification.
bank.ctx: This supports transgender rights: letting people have the law recognise the gender they identify as and access gender-affirming care. 'Self-identification' laws, used in countries like Ireland and Argentina, allow a legal gender change without medical gatekeeping. The stake is whether gender is defined by identity or by biology.

bank.q: Biological sex is a reality the law should not let a declaration override.
bank.ctx: This is the 'gender-critical' view: that biological sex is a fixed, binary reality no declaration or surgery can change, and that the law should rest on it — in single-sex spaces, sport, and official data. Associated with feminists like J.K. Rowling, it clashes head-on with the identity-based view.

bank.q: Workers need stronger unions and rights, and fair-pay agreements should return.
bank.ctx: 'Fair-pay agreements' set minimum pay and conditions across whole industries. This supports stronger unions and worker rights and bringing those agreements back after they were repealed. The stake is the balance of power between workers and employers.

bank.q: Union power and central pay deals hold the economy back and cost jobs.
bank.ctx: This argues union power and centrally negotiated pay deals hold the economy back and cost jobs. The stake is protecting workers versus business flexibility.

bank.q: Benefits are too low and should be raised to lift people out of poverty.
bank.ctx: This argues welfare benefits are too low and should be raised to lift people out of poverty. The stake is the adequacy of the safety net.

bank.q: Raising benefits too far just weakens the incentive to work.
bank.ctx: This argues raising benefits too far weakens the incentive to work. The stake is balancing support against work incentives.

bank.q: New Zealand over-regulates business; companies need far less red tape.
bank.ctx: This argues New Zealand over-regulates business and companies need far less red tape. The stake is whether deregulation would boost the economy.

bank.q: Cutting regulation just lets companies off the hook on workers and the environment.
bank.ctx: This argues cutting regulation just lets companies off the hook on workers and the environment. The stake is whether rules protect people or burden business.

bank.q: The tighter gun laws passed after the Christchurch attack were right and should stay.
bank.ctx: After the 2019 Christchurch terror attack, New Zealand swiftly banned most semi-automatic weapons. This supports keeping those tighter gun laws. The stake is public safety versus gun owners' rights.

bank.q: The post-Christchurch gun laws punished law-abiding owners and should be loosened.
bank.ctx: This argues the post-Christchurch gun laws punished law-abiding owners — farmers and sport shooters — without stopping criminals, and should be loosened. The stake is whether the ban targets the right people.

bank.q: Abortion is a settled right and access should be protected.
bank.ctx: This treats abortion — decriminalised and made a health matter in 2020 — as a settled right whose access should be protected. The stake is securing abortion access.

bank.q: Abortion ends a human life and the law is too permissive.
bank.ctx: This argues abortion ends a human life and the current law is too permissive. The stake is the moral status of the unborn.

bank.q: The legalisation of assisted dying was the right, compassionate choice.
bank.ctx: New Zealand legalised assisted dying for the terminally ill in 2021, after a public referendum. This defends that as the right, compassionate choice. The stake is control over one's own death.

bank.q: Assisted dying puts pressure on the vulnerable and crosses a line society should not cross.
bank.ctx: This argues assisted dying pressures the vulnerable and crosses a line society shouldn't cross. The stake is whether the safeguards protect the vulnerable.

bank.q: Drug use should be treated as a health issue, and cannabis legalised.
bank.ctx: This supports treating drug use as a health issue and legalising cannabis — which New Zealanders narrowly rejected in a 2020 referendum. The stake is whether prohibition or regulation better handles cannabis.

bank.q: Going soft on drugs fuels addiction and harm, and it should be reversed.
bank.ctx: This argues softening drug laws fuels addiction and harm and should be reversed. The stake is whether easing drug laws helps or hurts.

bank.q: New Zealand should take a harder line on China even at the cost of trade.
bank.ctx: This supports taking a harder line on China — a major trading partner but a strategic concern — even at the cost of trade. The stake is security versus economic dependence.

bank.q: New Zealand’s prosperity depends on trade with China, and confrontation would be reckless.
bank.ctx: This argues New Zealand's prosperity depends on trade with China, its largest market for dairy and other exports, so confrontation would be reckless. The stake is standing firm versus protecting trade.

bank.q: New Zealand should increase defence spending and align more closely with allies like AUKUS.
bank.ctx: This supports higher defence spending and aligning more closely with allies, such as the AUKUS security pact. The stake is whether New Zealand should shed some of its independent, nuclear-free stance.

bank.q: New Zealand should stay independent and nuclear-free, not be dragged into a military bloc.
bank.ctx: This argues New Zealand should stay independent and nuclear-free — a proud national position since the 1980s — rather than be pulled into a military bloc against China. The stake is independence versus alliance.

bank.q: Protecting nature should take priority over new mining and development.
bank.ctx: This puts protecting nature ahead of new mining and development, safeguarding New Zealand's 'clean, green' environment. The stake is conservation versus resource development.

bank.q: Endless environmental objections are strangling the projects New Zealand needs to prosper.
bank.ctx: This argues endless environmental objections are strangling the projects New Zealand needs. The stake is whether green rules protect nature or block growth.

bank.q: The government should intervene directly, with price controls, to ease the cost of living.
bank.ctx: This supports the government intervening with price controls to ease a sharp cost-of-living squeeze. The stake is how far the state should intervene in prices.

bank.q: Price controls just cause shortages; they don’t fix the cost of living.
bank.ctx: This argues price controls just cause shortages and don't fix the underlying causes. The stake is whether intervention helps or worsens the cost of living.

bank.q: Major decisions should be put to the people directly through binding referendums.
bank.ctx: This supports direct democracy: putting major decisions to the public in binding referendums, which New Zealand uses occasionally. The stake is whether big choices belong to voters or representatives.

bank.q: Referendums reduce complex questions to slogans and are easily hijacked by populists.
bank.ctx: This argues referendums reduce complex issues to slogans and are easily hijacked by populists. The stake is whether some decisions are too complex for a public vote.

bank.q: Public media like RNZ and TVNZ are worth their funding and must stay independent.
bank.ctx: RNZ and TVNZ are New Zealand's public media. This argues they are worth their funding and must stay independent. The stake is the value and independence of public broadcasting.

bank.q: Public broadcasters are biased and bloated, and their funding should be cut.
bank.ctx: This argues public broadcasters are biased and bloated and their funding should be cut. The stake is whether public media deserves its funding.

bank.q: Immigrants should adapt to New Zealand culture, not the other way around.
bank.ctx: This argues immigrants should adapt to New Zealand culture rather than the country adapting to them. The stake is how much cultural conformity to expect of newcomers.

bank.q: A living culture is always a blend; demanding assimilation impoverishes New Zealand.
bank.ctx: This argues a living culture is always a blend, so demanding assimilation impoverishes New Zealand. The stake is integration versus multiculturalism.

bank.q: Parents should have more control over what their children are taught about gender and identity.
bank.ctx: This argues parents should have more control over what schools teach their children about gender and identity. The stake is who controls sensitive parts of the curriculum.

bank.q: Curriculum should be set by educators and evidence, not by parental veto over inclusion.
bank.ctx: This argues the curriculum should be set by educators and evidence, not a parental veto over inclusive teaching. The stake is parental authority versus professional education.

bank.q: Free trade has made New Zealand richer and should be defended.
bank.ctx: This supports free trade as having made New Zealand, a small trading nation reliant on exports, richer. The stake is the value of economic openness.

bank.q: Free trade left New Zealand exposed and dependent, and communities behind.
bank.ctx: This argues free trade left New Zealand exposed and dependent, with communities left behind. The stake is who globalisation left behind.

bank.q: The unemployed are treated with too much suspicion; the safety net should be stronger.
bank.ctx: This argues the unemployed are treated with too much suspicion and the safety net should be stronger. The stake is how generous and accessible welfare should be.

bank.q: Welfare too easily becomes a trap, and sanctions protect taxpayers who fund it.
bank.ctx: This argues welfare can trap people, and sanctions protect the taxpayers who fund it. The stake is whether conditions on aid help or punish recipients.

bank.q: New Zealanders should feel able to express national pride without being called racist.
bank.ctx: This argues New Zealanders should be able to express national pride without being accused of racism. The stake is the space for patriotism in a country reckoning with its colonial past.

bank.q: Uncritical national pride glosses over colonisation and its ongoing harms.
bank.ctx: This argues uncritical national pride glosses over colonisation and its ongoing harms to Māori. The stake is patriotism versus honesty about the past.

bank.q: Long-standing traditions carry the wisdom of generations and should not be discarded lightly.
bank.ctx: This is the conservative philosophy of tradition, associated with Edmund Burke: that long-standing customs and institutions hold the accumulated, hard-won wisdom of generations, so change should be gradual and cautious rather than sweeping away what works for untested ideas.

bank.q: Worshipping tradition just lets the dead govern the living and blocks necessary change.
bank.ctx: This is the progressive reply, in the spirit of Thomas Paine's line that 'the dead should not govern the living': that treating tradition as sacred just lets the prejudices of the past block overdue reform — as appeals to tradition once defended slavery and denying women the vote.

bank.q: A good society depends more on personal responsibility than on government support.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core right-leaning value: that a healthy society depends mainly on individuals taking responsibility for their own choices and lives, and that leaning too heavily on government breeds dependence and saps initiative.

bank.q: Blaming individuals for problems the system creates is how the comfortable excuse others’ suffering.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core left-leaning value: that many hardships — poverty, poor health, joblessness — stem from unfair systems and circumstances beyond personal control, so blaming individuals lets the comfortable ignore problems they benefit from or could help fix.

context:
Politics in New Zealand: the landscape behind this test

New Zealand replaced first-past-the-post with mixed-member proportional representation in 1996, and the change reshaped its politics. Voters cast two votes, one for a local candidate and one for a party, with the party vote determining overall seat share. Single-party majorities are now rare, so governing means negotiating.

The party system

Labour and National remain the two largest parties and the only realistic sources of a prime minister, but neither can usually govern alone. The Greens sit to Labour's left on economics and environment. ACT advances a classical liberal, small-state programme. New Zealand First occupies a populist position that has supported governments of both major parties. Te Pati Maori advocates for Maori rights and constitutional change.

Because coalition partners are needed, smaller parties translate modest vote shares into real policy concessions, and coalition agreements are published documents that shape the government's programme.

The cleavages that actually divide voters

The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840, is central to New Zealand's constitutional arrangements and to its most contested arguments. Questions about co-governance, the role of te reo Maori in public life, and how Treaty obligations bind government are genuinely divisive in a way that has no close parallel abroad.

Housing affordability is persistently among the most severe in the developed world and dominates domestic debate. Agriculture's central economic role also makes climate policy unusually complicated, since a large share of emissions comes from farming rather than energy.

How this maps onto the compass

New Zealand built an extensive welfare state, then executed one of the most rapid market liberalisations in the OECD during the 1980s. The result is a mixed settlement: public healthcare and income support alongside comparatively open markets. On social questions the country is permissive by international standards.

This test asks about New Zealand policy, including Treaty questions. For the full profiles, see the New Zealand party guides.
